strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: converting dense LLM checkpoints into MoE architectures without expensive continual pre-training, enabling rapid deployment under compute constraints.

The training-free, analytically constructed router is the most novel element. Formulating router construction as a minimization problem and deriving an approximate solution from activation statistics (rather than training a router from scratch) is a genuine technical contribution over prior work like MoEfication and MoEBERT.
The balanced K-means formulation reduced to a balanced linear assignment problem (via the extended distance matrix) is well-motivated and formally specified, aiding reproducibility.

Comprehensive evaluation: perplexity on WikiText-2/C4, six downstream benchmarks, measured end-to-end latency on real hardware (Table 3), ablations on fine-tuning data size, expert configurations, load balancing, calibration data size (Appendix B), and scaling to Llama-2 13B (Appendix C).

Comparison against both strong parameter-partition baselines (LLaMA-MoE, LLaMA-MoE-v2) and dense-small models (Pythia-1.0B, TinyLlama-1.1B, Table 4) gives useful context on knowledge transfer from the base model.
Hyperparameters, calibration procedure, and optimizer settings are documented in enough detail to reproduce the pipeline.
weaknesses: Overclaiming in the abstract and conclusion: the 75% activation configuration is described as 'lossless precision,' but Table 1 shows WikiText-2 PPL of 7.02 vs. 5.27 for the dense model (a ~33% degradation), and the corresponding speedup is only 5%. This characterization is not supported by the evidence.

Key theoretical steps rest on heuristic assumptions that are asserted rather than rigorously validated: the approximation argmin|hi*wdown,i| ≈ argmin|hi| (Eq. 3) and the chain of approximations in Eq. 13. The only support is an empirical histogram in Appendix A, which is thin for a paper whose central contribution is an 'analytical' construction.

The choice Ka = 10 for ATopK is admitted to 'sound counter-intuitive but works best in practice,' with no sensitivity analysis or explanation, weakening confidence that the activation criterion is well understood.

Baseline fairness is unclear. LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 were produced via continual pre-training on large corpora, yet they are evaluated here in training-free form or after only a 2k-sample LoRA fine-tune, and appear to collapse (PPL > 10k, NaN). The comparison protocol is not fully explained, making the headline superiority over baselines hard to interpret; an apples-to-apples comparison (e.g., same fine-tuning budget for all methods, or against the published continually-pretrained checkpoints) is needed.

Training-free 25% activation PPL of ~60 (WikiText-2) vs. 5.27 dense is severely degraded; the practical claim of 'immediate deployment' at aggressive sparsity is weakened, and downstream accuracy at 25% activation remains far below dense even after 2k fine-tuning.

Writing quality is below publication standard: duplicated text ('Based on continual training, [12] modifies [12] modifies'), garbled text ('oo deease the embedding dimension'), typos ('perpective'), and the code URL in the abstract is empty, harming reproducibility claims at submission time.

Speedup evaluation is limited to a single GPU and small batch regimes; the claimed benefit is largest in 'large batch size scenarios' per the motivation, but compute-bound batch configurations are underexplored relative to that framing.

Only Llama-2/Llama-3 (ReLU-free SwiGLU) architectures are tested despite related work noting that sparse-activation phenomena differ across activation functions; generality of the method across model families is unestablished.

strengths: The core idea is practical and well-motivated: a training-free dense-to-MoE conversion that completes in minutes, with an analytic router construction formulated as a minimization problem (Eq. 12-16), which is a more principled treatment than ad-hoc router initialization in prior work.

The balanced-assignment formulation of expert clustering (Eq. 7-10), including the matrix extension trick to reduce the unbalanced problem to a standard balanced assignment, is technically clean and well described.

Experiments cover multiple axes: PPL on two models and two corpora, six downstream benchmarks, measured end-to-end latency under both memory- and compute-bound settings, ablations on calibration data size, expert configuration, load balancing, and scaling to Llama-2 13B (Appendix C).

The framework is honest about some trade-offs in places: training-free 25% activation degrades substantially, and extended fine-tuning results (Table 4) are reported even when CMoE underperforms pre-trained dense-small models.
The problem (cheap upcycling of dense checkpoints into sparse FFNs) is relevant to efficient NLP deployment and within scope for ACL.
weaknesses: Overclaiming in the headline results. The abstract and conclusion claim 'lossless precision in terms of perplexity' at 75% activation, but Table 1 shows WikiText-2 PPL of 7.02 vs. dense 5.27 (and C4 10.98 vs. 7.27) — a roughly 30-50% relative degradation that is clearly not lossless. For this degraded quality the method delivers only a 5% end-to-end speedup, which undercuts the central value proposition.

The 'usable perplexity' claim at 25% activation is questionable: training-free PPL of ~60-140 and downstream accuracies far below dense (e.g., BoolQ 46 vs. 82, HellaSwag 30 vs. 79) are not practically usable without fine-tuning, yet the framing treats these as a working configuration.
The >76% recovery statistic is cherry-picked from the two best benchmarks (SciQ and BoolQ); on HellaSwag and WinoGrande the recovery is much lower, and the abstract's framing does not disclose this.

Unfair baseline treatment. LLaMA-MoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 were designed to be used with continual pre-training; evaluating them in a training-free regime and then reporting 'catastrophic degradation' makes the baselines look far worse than their published performance. The comparison after 2k LoRA fine-tuning is more informative, but the headline narrative relies on the training-free comparison.

Several derivations rest on unstated or weakly justified approximations: hypothesis (3) (argmin of |h_i * w_down,i| approx argmin |h_i|), the assumption that h_i values are independent across neurons, and the step from (13) to (14)-(15) which assumes the router can freely control the ordering of expected expert activations. No empirical validation of these assumptions beyond a single histogram (Figure A.1) is provided.

Writing and polish problems undermine confidence: the code URL in the abstract is empty ('available at .'), the related-work section contains a duplicated citation ('[12] modifies [12] modifies...'), the garbled sentence 'SliceGPT ... oo deease the embedding dimension', and typos such as 'from the perpective'. Reference [3] (visual instruction tuning) is cited as an example of scaling LLMs, which is inappropriate.

Calibration-data sensitivity is acknowledged but downplayed: Tables B.1 and C.1 show large swings (e.g., Llama-2 13B WikiText-2 PPL 56.25 with WT-2 calibration vs. 116.77 with C4), meaning the method's training-free quality is strongly domain-dependent, which limits the generality of the claims.

Limited architectural generality: only Llama-family models with SwiGLU FFNs are tested; no evidence the approach transfers to GELU/ReLU FFNs or other architectures, and the ATonK hyperparameter choice (K_a=10) is justified only as 'sounds counter-intuitive but works best in practice'.

The claimed novelty over MoEfication and related neuron-partition work is incremental: activation-based shared/routed splitting and clustering neurons by co-activation both have close precedents; the main differentiators are the balanced assignment and the analytic router, which alone may not warrant main-conference novelty.

strengths: The training-free conversion problem is well motivated: converting dense LLMs to MoEs without costly continual pre-training is practically relevant, and the paper targets a genuine gap (existing conversion methods require heavy retraining).

The analytical router construction (Section 3.2) is the most interesting technical component: formulating router construction as a minimization problem and deriving an approximate solution from representative-neuron activation statistics is a clearer and more principled approach than heuristic hidden-feature initialization used in prior work.

The balanced K-means clustering via a linear-assignment reduction (Jonker-Volgenant) with the column-extension trick is a clean formulation, and the methodology is described at a level of detail that is largely reproducible (calibration setup, LoRA hyperparameters, load-balancing mechanism).

The evaluation covers multiple axes (PPL on WikiText-2/C4, six downstream tasks, measured end-to-end latency on both memory- and compute-bound settings) and includes useful ablations: fine-tuning data size, calibration data size (Appendix B), scaling to 13B (Appendix C), expert configuration, and load balancing.
Honest reporting of some negative results, e.g., training-free CMoE underperforms small dense models (Table 4) and a candid Limitations discussion.
Code release is promised, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. 'Lossless precision in terms of perplexity' at 75% activation is contradicted by Table 1 (WikiText-2 PPL 7.02 vs. dense 5.27 training-free; 5.69 vs. 5.27 after fine-tuning — still a gap). Calling PPL ~62-136 training-free at 25% activation 'usable perplexity' is also generous, and the 5% acceleration at 75% activation is marginal.

The baseline comparison framing is potentially unfair/misleading. LLaMA-MoE is a method explicitly designed around continual pre-training; evaluating it with only a 2k-sample LoRA fine-tune (Table 1 shows catastrophic PPL) and presenting it as an inferior alternative conflates 'designed for training-free use' with 'broken under a setting it was never built for'. The strong version of the contribution would be a comparison after each baseline receives its intended post-training budget.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the abstract/main text state the default 25% configuration is S1A1E8, yet Table 1's CMoE 25% row (62.30/12.73) matches the S2A2E16 row of Table 5 rather than S1A1E8 (60.86/12.76). Figure 1's label 'Inference of FMoE' appears to be a typo for CMoE. The code URL in the abstract is missing (blank after 'available at .').

The writing has multiple defects suggesting insufficient proofreading: e.g., '[12] modifies [12] modifies the LLaMA-2 7B model' (p.2), 'substitutes each weight matrix with a smaller dense matrix oo deease the embedding dimension', 'the output of original output of the dense FFN' (p.5), 'from the perpective of the perplexity' (Conclusion).

The derivations rest on several stacked heuristic approximations (Eq. 3 hypothesis, the norm-sparsity equivalence in Eq. 13, the representative-neuron assumption h_r_Rj ≈ h̄_j in Eq. 19) that are asserted rather than empirically validated; no experiment directly tests how well the analytical router approximates the optimum or how sensitive results are to these assumptions.

Hyperparameter choices are under-justified: Ka=10 'sounds counter-intuitive but works best in practice' is given without analysis; the router learning rate (0.001) and LoRA rate (5.95e-5) appear tuned without sensitivity discussion; all results appear to be single-run with no variance or significance reporting, notable given the 8-sample calibration.

Novelty over the closest prior work (MoEfication, MoEBERT, Deja Vu) is incremental: activation-based neuron grouping and shared/routed decomposition are established ideas; the main deltas are balanced assignment and the analytical router.
Empirical claims about speedup lack detail (GPU model, batch sizes, kernel implementation for sparse FFN), making the latency numbers hard to reproduce or contextualize.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core observation: FFN neuron activation frequencies exhibit a bimodal structure (consistently active vs. conditionally active neurons), which the authors show prior FFN-to-MoE methods ignore; Figure 2 and the domain-invariance overlap analysis (84-86% shared-neuron overlap across math/code/science domains) support that this structure is intrinsic rather than a calibration artifact.

Practical and efficient method: the analytical restructuring requires only ~8 calibration examples and minutes of computation (4.5 min construction on Llama-2 7B), with a training-free variant that already outperforms fine-tuned baselines (42.50 vs 38.02 MMLU), a genuinely useful property for practitioners.

Broad and reasonably fair empirical evaluation across four model families (Llama-2 7B/70B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-30B-A3B, plus Qwen-2.5-72B for speedup), consistent gains at 25% sparsity, and baselines reimplemented under matched 2k-sample fine-tuning budgets.

Good ablation design: Table 5 cleanly isolates the contributions of analytical routing vs. activation-based clustering with shared experts (+2-6 pp and +5-7 pp respectively), and the method is shown orthogonal to neuron-level sparsity (WINA) and applicable hierarchically to existing MoE models.

Appendix provides complete derivations of the activation profiling pipeline, balanced clustering (with a clean L2/Hamming equivalence argument), and the router construction, plus honest limitations (calibration dependence, generation variance, English/decoder-only scope).
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: the core idea of routing by activation patterns descends directly from MoEfication/G-MoEfication, and separating always-active neurons into structurally distinct shared experts echoes DeepSeek-MoE-style shared experts and MoE-BERT's importance sharing; the paper's delta over this prior line is real but incremental, and the related-work positioning, while thorough, does not fully sharpen what is fundamentally new.

The theoretical justification is heuristic rather than rigorous: the central hypothesis (Eq. 12, arg min |h_i * w_i| ≈ arg min |h_i|) ignores the substantial variation of down-projection column magnitudes and inter-neuron output cancellation; the L1 hidden-state-magnitude proxy (Eq. 23) and the 'representative neuron' router (one neuron per expert) are approximations whose quality is never quantified (e.g., no measurement of router score vs. true expert contribution correlation).
No variance reporting: results are single-run numbers without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite the gains over EMoE sometimes being modest (e.g., ~1 pp MMLU in Table 2).

Efficiency gains are modest and deployment-dependent: ~15% throughput improvement for 25% FFN sparsity, and wall-clock speedups (up to 1.17x) are reported on only one model in a limited regime; no discussion of kernel/implementation maturity needed to realize MoE speedups at small expert counts in memory-bound settings.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a method whose value hinges on practical deployment; several implementation details (clustering convergence, exact KV/cache handling during profiling) would need the released pipeline to verify.

Baseline comparability caveat: LLaMA-MoE v1/v2 are continual-pretraining methods evaluated far outside their intended token budget regime; while matched-budget comparison is defensible, the headline 'orders of magnitude more resources' framing partly compares against strawman operating points, and the reported LLaMA-MoE degradation at 2k samples (e.g., 49.35 PIQA) suggests the baselines were not designed for this setting rather than being strictly inferior methods.

Minor clarity issues: the Sparsity column in Table 1 mixes 0/20/25% without per-table emphasis, the claim that 0.125 sparsity slightly beats dense PPL ('implicit regularization') is speculative and under-supported, and some benchmark details (few-shot prompts, eval harness) are unspecified.

strengths: The paper is clearly written, and the central observation — FFN neurons split into a consistently active group and an input-conditional group — is empirically grounded (Figures 1-2) and motivating for an analytical, post-hoc MoE construction.

The proposed method is simple and practical: shared/routed expert partitioning from activation rates plus an analytical router built from representative neurons avoids router training, with a useful load-balancing bias mechanism that requires no auxiliary loss.

The experimental coverage is broad for this line of work: four models from 7B to 72B (including an existing MoE model for hierarchical restructuring), five zero-shot benchmarks plus MMLU/HumanEval/GSM8K, ablations on calibration size/source, clustering vs. routing contributions, and FLOPs/throughput measurements including composition with WINA.

Ablation Table 5 is a genuine attempt to isolate contributions, showing the analytical router and activation-based clustering with shared experts each contribute independently over MoEfication/G-MoEfication/Read-ME under matched settings.

The comparison of token budgets and conversion times (Table 6) fairly acknowledges that LLaMA-MoE does continual pre-training while this work does post-training restructuring, and the limitations section is candid about calibration dependence, generation variance, and the English/decoder-only scope.
weaknesses: The achieved operating point is modest. At the headline 25% sparsity, downstream accuracy still falls well below the dense baseline on every benchmark and every model (e.g., Llama-2 7B: 74.34 vs 78.78 PIQA, 40.35 vs 46.16 ARC-C, 65.77 vs 69.06 WinoGrande), and the speedup is only 1.17x in the most favorable compute-bound setting — a narrow margin over structured pruning baselines that were given a lower sparsity target.

The perplexity-sparsity trade-off (Table 10) is severely degraded outside a narrow window: PPL rises from 5.27 (dense) to 6.55/7.71/9.56/12.73 at 0.375-0.75 sparsity. The claim that 0.125 sparsity slightly outperforms dense PPL 'may provide implicit regularization' is speculative and unexplained; a result this surprising (a lossy restructuring beating the original) needs much stronger analysis than a one-line conjecture.

The core theoretical justification is weak. The sparsity hypothesis (Eq. 12, 'arg min_i |h_i w_down,i| ≈ arg min_i |h_i|') is hand-wavy: it is stated as an approximation of an arg min but effectively used as an ordering assumption, and it ignores that w_down magnitudes differ systematically across clusters — precisely the quantity that determines an expert's true output contribution. Eq. 23 inherits this gap, so the 'analytical' router's optimality claim (Eq. 24) is not rigorously supported.

All baselines are re-implemented and re-fine-tuned by the authors rather than taken from prior reports, and structured pruning baselines are run at 20% vs the proposed method's 25% FFN-only sparsity. While the paper argues the effective sparsities are comparable, this asymmetry, combined with author-run baselines, makes the central 'outperforms prior methods' claim hard to verify against the literature.

Novelty is incremental. Activation-based neuron grouping into experts, top-K activation profiling, and co-activation clustering are all established (MoEfication, G-MoEfication, DejaVu, TEAL); the distinct contributions — separating high-frequency neurons into structurally separate shared experts and the representative-neuron router — are deltas on that template, and the shared-expert design echoes DeepSeek-MoE.

Reproducibility is not assured: no code release is mentioned anywhere, results are single-run with no variance or significance reporting, and several results (Table 2, Table 3) are reported only on Llama-2 7B rather than across models.

The paper's framing slightly overstates the result: 'enabling immediate deployment' is undercut by the substantial training-free quality gap (42.50 MMLU vs 46.16-level dense numbers on other tasks) and the need for 2k-sample fine-tuning plus load balancing to reach reported numbers.

Some experimental details are under-specified for reproduction, e.g., how the Jonker-Volgenant balanced assignment scales to thousands of neurons per layer (claimed O(n^3)), and how the hierarchical sub-routers interact with the load-balancing biases in the Qwen3-30B-A3B experiments.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated observation: the bimodal distribution of neuron activation rates (consistently-active vs. conditionally-active neurons) is empirically demonstrated (Figures 1-2) and convincingly used to justify separating shared from routed experts, addressing a genuine shortcoming of prior uniform-treatment FFN-to-MoE methods.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning four models (Llama-2 7B/70B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-30B-A3B) plus an industrial-scale speedup study on Qwen-2.5-72B, covering zero-shot tasks, MMLU/HumanEval/GSM8K, and perplexity — much broader than typical papers in this area.

Thorough ablations: Table 5 cleanly disentangles the contributions of activation-based clustering vs. the analytical router (with controlled cross-combinations on MoEfication/G-MoEfication/Read-ME); calibration-source/size sensitivity (Table 4) and domain-overlap analysis (84-86% shared-neuron overlap across math/science/code) support the claim that shared-expert selection is intrinsic rather than domain-specific.

Practically compelling efficiency story: 4.5 minutes analytical construction and 46-minute end-to-end time versus days-to-weeks for LLaMA-MoE baselines; orthogonality with neuron-level sparsity (WINA) and hierarchical application to existing MoE models broaden applicability.

Appendix provides complete mathematical derivations (sparsity hypothesis, balanced clustering via Jonker-Volgenant, router construction) and implementation details (LoRA configuration, load-balancing gamma, ATopK with Ka=10), which aids reproducibility of the method description.
weaknesses: All baselines are reimplemented by the authors and fine-tuned with only a 2k-sample budget. Methods like LLaMA-MoE-v1/v2 were designed for 200B/7B-token continual pre-training; evaluating them under a 2k-sample regime plausibly handicaps them, and the paper's headline 'orders of magnitude fewer resources' comparison (Table 6) is partly a consequence of this setup rather than a like-for-like algorithmic comparison. The large gaps over LLaMA-MoE (e.g., 25.77 vs 69.36 HellaSwag) should be interpreted cautiously.

No evidence of released code or artifacts, and no reproducibility statement. Given that all baselines are re-implementations and several hyperparameters matter (Ka, expert configurations like S3A3E8, gamma, LoRA settings), independent verification is difficult.

Absolute quality degradation remains substantial: on Llama-2 7B, PIQA drops from 78.78 to 74.34 and HellaSwag from 76.00 to 69.36 at 25% sparsity; perplexity at 0.5 sparsity is 7.71 vs 5.27 dense. The gains over the strongest baseline (EMoE) are consistent but moderate (e.g., +1.9 PIQA, +2.0 ARC-C), and no variance/significance reporting is provided.

The theoretical justification is heuristic: the central hypothesis (Eq. 12, argmin |h_i w_i| ≈ argmin |h_i|) is asserted informally, and the reduction of reconstruction error to expert hidden-state L1 magnitude (Eq. 23) involves unquantified approximations; there is no empirical validation of how well the single representative neuron's activation tracks actual expert contribution.

The headline 'up to 1.17× speedup' arises only in a specific configuration (Qwen-2.5-72B, batch size >400, 32k context, S1A5E8); the more representative Llama-2 7B throughput gain is 14.8%, and abstract framing slightly overstates typical results.

Some analysis sections mix evidence with speculation (e.g., the converted model slightly beating dense at 0.125 sparsity attributed to 'implicit regularization'; the self-consistency variance argument), and the paper would benefit from clearer discussion of why the analytical router suffices versus a trained router at matched budget.

Evaluation is limited to English, decoder-only architectures; the limitations section acknowledges this, but the claimed generality of the 'activation pattern' observation is tested on only two model families.
